etymology: From the Dutch city of Dordrecht, where the great international Reformed synod sat in the years 1618 and 1619.
biblical_def: The Synod of Dort was the great international assembly of the Reformed churches, convened at Dordrecht in the Netherlands from November 1618 to May 1619, gathering not only the Dutch divines but delegates from England, Scotland, the Palatinate, Switzerland, and the German Reformed lands. Its occasion was the rise of the Arminian party, who in the Remonstrance of 1610 had assailed the doctrines of sovereign grace. Against them the Synod set forth its Canons, which answered the five articles of the Remonstrants point for point, and which the church has since gathered under the heads of total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, irresistible grace, and the perseverance of the saints. These are not the inventions of men but the plain teaching of Scripture: that the Father gives a people to the Son, and all that He giveth shall come (Joh 6:37); that God hath mercy on whom He will have mercy, not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth (Rom 9:15–16); that He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4–5); and that none shall pluck His sheep out of His hand (Joh 10:28–29). The Canons of Dort stand among the Three Forms of Unity, a faithful confession of the gospel of grace alone, and the dictionary honours them as a true and Scriptural defence of the God who saves to the uttermost.
webster_summary: The great international Reformed synod of 1618–19 whose Canons answered the Arminians and confessed the doctrines of sovereign grace.
webster_full: SYNOD OF DORT, the international Reformed assembly at Dordrecht, 1618–19.
It was convened to answer the Arminian Remonstrants and their five articles.
Its Canons set forth the doctrines of sovereign and effectual grace.
These are gathered under five heads: depravity, election, atonement, grace, perseverance.
The Canons stand among the Three Forms of Unity of the Reformed churches.
scriptures: Joh 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
Rom 9:15
For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
corruption_summary: Dort confessed sovereign grace against the Arminian corruption that made salvation hang upon the will of man.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption the Synod of Dort answered was the Arminianism of the Remonstrants, who taught that election rests upon foreseen faith, that Christ died alike for all without effectually saving any, that grace may be finally resisted, and that the believer may fall away and perish. This was a corruption of the gospel of grace, for it removed the cause of salvation from the free mercy of God and lodged it in the will and choice of man. Dort named the error and condemned it, not as a difference of emphasis but as a departure from the Scripture that makes God, not man, the author and finisher of salvation.

The dictionary honours the Canons of Dort as a true confession and warns against the perennial return of the same error in modern dress. Wherever it is taught that God chose because He foresaw faith, or that the cross only made salvation possible until man completed it by his decision, or that the regenerate may yet be lost, the Remonstrance is preached again under a new name. Against all such teaching the Canons stand, confessing that salvation is of the LORD from first to last, and that He will lose none whom the Father hath given to His Son.
roots_summary: Named from Dordrecht, the synod gave the Reformed churches their Canons on the doctrines of grace.
roots_lines: Dort — from the Dutch city of Dordrecht.
The synod sat from November 1618 to May 1619.
It gathered delegates from across the Reformed churches of Europe.
Its Canons answered the five articles of the Remonstrants.
The Canons stand among the Three Forms of Unity.
usage: Like the divines of Dort, the church must answer error not with compromise but with Scripture.
Dort teaches that salvation is of the LORD from first to last, not hanging upon the will of man.
The Canons confess a God who saves a people to the uttermost and loses none of His own.

etymology: From the town of Herborn in the county of Nassau, where the Reformed academy was founded in 1584.
biblical_def: The Herborn Academy was a Reformed school of higher learning founded in 1584 in the town of Herborn in Nassau, under the patronage of Count John VI, a zealous patron of the Reformed faith. Though never granted the formal rank of a university, it became one of the great nurseries of Reformed scholasticism and covenant theology in the German lands. Its first rector was Caspar Olevianus, co-author of the Heidelberg Catechism, and among its teachers were Johannes Piscator, the careful commentator and translator of the Herborn Bible, and Johann Heinrich Alsted, the encyclopaedist whose ordered learning bound all knowledge under the service of God. To Herborn also came, as a young student, John Amos Comenius, the great teacher of the Bohemian Brethren. The academy laboured to hand down sound doctrine from one generation to the next, after the pattern Paul gave to Timothy: “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Such a school is a fruit of the command to teach diligently the things of God to the rising generation (Deu 6:7), that all Scripture, given by inspiration of God and profitable for doctrine, might furnish the man of God unto every good work (2Ti 3:16). Herborn stands as a witness to the Reformed care for learning made the servant of godliness.
webster_summary: The Reformed academy in Nassau founded 1584, home of Olevianus, Piscator, and Alsted, a nursery of covenant theology.
webster_full: HERBORN ACADEMY, a Reformed school founded 1584 in Nassau.
It was a nursery of Reformed scholasticism and covenant theology.
Caspar Olevianus, co-author of the Heidelberg Catechism, was its first rector.
Piscator and Alsted taught there; young Comenius studied there.
It laboured to hand sound doctrine to the rising generation.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: A Reformed school of learning, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to sound learning made the servant of godliness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Reformed care for learning made the handmaid of godliness. Herborn gathered Olevianus, Piscator, and Alsted to teach sound doctrine, and committed it to faithful men who should be able to teach others also. Learning is not an end in itself nor a worldly ornament; it is a trust to be handed down, that the truth of God might be guarded and passed whole to the generation following.

Herborn also commends the labour of catechising and the binding of all knowledge under the service of God. Olevianus, who helped frame the Heidelberg Catechism, knew that the rising generation must be taught diligently the things of the LORD; Alsted laboured to order all learning unto one end, the glory of God. Where the schools of men today divorce knowledge from godliness and learning from the fear of the LORD, Herborn stands as a witness that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the LORD, and that every art and science is rightly studied only in His light.
roots_summary: Named from the town of Herborn in Nassau, the Reformed academy founded there in 1584.
roots_lines: Herborn — a town in the county of Nassau.

usage: Like Herborn, sound doctrine must be committed to faithful men able to teach others also.
The academy teaches that learning is rightly pursued only as the handmaid of godliness.

etymology: From the Latin remonstrare, “to protest” or “to show again,” after the Remonstrance they issued in 1610.
biblical_def: The Remonstrants were the Arminian party in the Dutch Reformed Church, the followers of Jacobus Arminius, who after his death in 1609 gathered under Johannes Uytenbogaert and Simon Episcopius. In the year 1610 they presented to the States of Holland a document called the Remonstrance, setting forth five articles in which they departed from the received Reformed doctrine of grace. They taught conditional election grounded in foreseen faith; a universal atonement in which Christ died for all men alike though it saved none with certainty; a grace that may be finally resisted by the will of man; and they left in doubt whether the regenerate might fall away and perish. These articles overthrew the gospel of sovereign mercy, for they removed the saving cause from God and lodged it in the free choice of fallen man, contrary to the plain word that it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16); that whom He did predestinate, them He also called, and justified, and glorified (Rom 8:29–30); that we are saved by grace through faith, and that not of ourselves, lest any man should boast (Eph 2:8–9); and that Christ said, Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you (Joh 15:16). At the Synod of Dort the Remonstrant articles were weighed and condemned, and the Canons of Dort answered them with the doctrines of sovereign grace.
webster_summary: The Arminian party who issued the 1610 Remonstrance with its five articles, condemned at Dort as a corruption of sovereign grace.
webster_full: THE REMONSTRANTS, the Arminian party in the Dutch Reformed Church.
They followed Arminius, gathering under Uytenbogaert and Episcopius.
In 1610 they issued the Remonstrance with its five articles.
They taught conditional election, universal atonement, and resistible grace.
Their articles were condemned at the Synod of Dort.
scriptures: Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:

Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
corruption_summary: The Remonstrants corrupted sovereign grace, making election rest on foreseen faith and salvation hang upon the will of man.
corruption_paragraphs: The Remonstrants are themselves the corruption this entry names. Their five articles overthrew the doctrine of sovereign grace at every point: election was made to rest upon faith which God foresaw, rather than faith being the gift that flows from election; the atonement was emptied of its saving power, made a possibility for all rather than a redemption that effectually saves the elect; and grace was made resistible, so that the last word in salvation belonged not to God but to man. This is the ancient error of human merit and free will, dressed in Reformed language, and it was rightly condemned.

The dictionary names Arminianism as a corruption, not a tolerable difference, because it strikes at the heart of the gospel. If God chose me because I would believe, then the glory of my salvation is divided with my own will; if Christ died no more for me than for those who perish, then the cross saves no one in particular; if grace may be finally refused, then no sinner could ever be saved, for the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God. Against the Remonstrants, Scripture lodges the whole of salvation in the free and sovereign mercy of God, that no flesh should glory in His presence.
roots_summary: Named from the 1610 Remonstrance, the Arminian protest against the Reformed doctrine of grace.
roots_lines: Remonstrants — from Latin remonstrare, “to protest.”
Named from the Remonstrance they issued in 1610.
They were the followers of Jacobus Arminius.
They set forth five articles against the doctrines of grace.
They were condemned at the Synod of Dort.
usage: Like the divines who answered the Remonstrants, the church must name Arminian error as a corruption of grace.
The Remonstrants teach the danger of lodging any part of salvation in the will of fallen man.
Their condemnation at Dort confirms that salvation is of the LORD, that no flesh should glory before Him.

etymology: From Latin generalis, “of the whole,” and assembly, a gathering called together; the highest court of Presbyterian polity.
biblical_def: In Presbyterian polity the General Assembly is the highest of the church courts, gathering ministers and ruling elders from the whole communion to deliberate, to judge appeals, and to maintain the peace and purity of the church. It rises above the session, the presbytery, and the synod, and is the visible bond of a connectional church, after the pattern the Presbyterian reads in the council at Jerusalem, where the apostles and elders came together to consider a weighty matter, and decreed what seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to them (Act 15:6, 28). The Scriptures honour the gathering of the elders to take counsel and the doing of all things decently and in order (1Co 14:40), and the dictionary honours the gravity and good order of the Presbyterian courts. Yet the phrase rises higher still, for the Holy Ghost speaks of a heavenly General Assembly: the believer is come “unto the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven” (Heb 12:23), gathered unto mount Sion, the city of the living God. The earthly courts are but shadows of that great congregation of the redeemed. Here the dictionary speaks plainly of its own confession: the 1689 London Baptist Confession holds that government is committed to each local congregation under its own elders (LBCF 26), not to a hierarchy of courts; yet it esteems the brotherly counsel of the churches together, and honours all that is decent, orderly, and Scriptural in the Presbyterian way.
webster_summary: The highest court of Presbyterian polity; and the heavenly assembly and church of the firstborn written in heaven (Heb 12:23).
webster_full: GENERAL ASSEMBLY, the highest court in Presbyterian polity.
It gathers ministers and ruling elders from the whole communion.
It rises above session, presbytery, and synod as the bond of a connectional church.
The Baptist holds instead to local-church congregational government (LBCF 26).
Scripture names a heavenly “general assembly and church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23).
scriptures: But ye are come unto mount Sion, and unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels,
To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, which are written in heaven, and to God the Judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: Honoured for its order and counsel, the Presbyterian court differs from the Baptist's congregational government, which the dictionary confesses (LBCF 26).
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter here is not a postmodern grievance but an honest difference of polity among brethren who hold one gospel. The Presbyterian General Assembly is a grave and orderly court, and the dictionary honours its care to do all things decently and in order, after the example of the apostles and elders gathered at Jerusalem. The principle to recover is that Christ governs His church by appointed officers and orderly counsel, not by the whim of the crowd nor the will of one prelate.

Yet the dictionary confesses the 1689 London Baptist position: that the Lord Jesus has given power and authority to each particular congregation, gathered according to His mind, to carry on its own government under its own elders, and that the highest court on earth is the assembled local church (LBCF 26). This is not named a corruption but an honest difference from the Presbyterian connectional courts; both are far removed from the true corruption, which is the popish hierarchy that set one man over the whole church. The clearest General Assembly remains the one no man convenes — the church of the firstborn, written in heaven, gathered unto mount Sion.
roots_summary: The highest Presbyterian court, and the heavenly assembly of the firstborn written in heaven.
roots_lines: General Assembly — from Latin generalis, “of the whole.”
In Presbyterian polity it is the highest of the church courts.
It rises above session, presbytery, and synod.
The Baptist holds to local-church congregational government (LBCF 26).
Scripture names the heavenly assembly and church of the firstborn (Heb 12:23).
usage: Like the apostles at Jerusalem, the church takes grave matters in orderly counsel under appointed officers.
The Baptist honours the Presbyterian courts yet confesses the local congregation's own government (LBCF 26).
The truest General Assembly is the church of the firstborn, written in heaven, gathered unto mount Sion.

etymology: From Latin sessio, “a sitting,” the sitting of the elders to govern the congregation.
biblical_def: In Presbyterian polity the session is the local court of a congregation, the lowest and nearest of the church courts, made up of the minister and the ruling elders, who sit together to oversee, to govern, and to shepherd the flock entrusted to them. The name marks the sitting of the elders to do the work of government, judging matters of discipline, admitting and watching over members, and caring for the souls of the people. This rests upon the New Testament pattern of a plurality of elders in every church, for Paul and Barnabas ordained elders in every church (Act 14:23), Paul left Titus in Crete to ordain elders in every city (Tit 1:5), and the elders who rule well are counted worthy of double honour (1Ti 5:17). Peter, himself an elder, charged the elders to feed the flock of God which is among them, taking the oversight thereof not by constraint but willingly (1Pe 5:1–2). The dictionary honours the plurality of elders as the true New Testament order, and rejoices in the Presbyterian care for ordered eldership. It marks honestly the Baptist difference: the 1689 Confession holds that the elders govern within and under the particular congregation, which has its own authority under Christ, rather than as the lowest rung of a hierarchy of courts. In both, the abiding truth is that Christ rules His church not by one lordly bishop nor by the unled multitude, but by a plurality of godly elders set over the flock.
webster_summary: In Presbyterian polity the local court of the minister and ruling elders governing a congregation; resting on the NT plurality of elders.
webster_full: SESSION, in Presbyterian polity the local court of the elders.
It is made up of the minister and the ruling elders of a congregation.
It oversees discipline, membership, and the shepherding of the flock.
It rests upon the New Testament plurality of elders (Act 14:23; Tit 1:5).
The Baptist holds the elders govern within the congregation's own authority.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Resting on the NT plurality of elders, the Presbyterian session differs from the Baptist's congregational government, both far from prelacy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the New Testament plurality of elders, against both the single lordly bishop and the leaderless crowd. The Presbyterian session embodies this rightly: a body of elders, not one ruler, set over the flock to feed and to govern it. The dictionary honours the Presbyterian care for ordered eldership and discipline, which guards the church from the tyranny of one man and the chaos of the ungoverned many alike.

The honest difference with the Baptist lies not in the eldership but in the courts above it. The 1689 Confession holds that the elders govern within the particular congregation, which itself has authority under Christ to carry on its own affairs, rather than as the lowest court answerable upward to presbytery, synod, and assembly. This is named a difference among brethren, not a corruption; the true corruption against which both stand is prelacy, the lifting of one bishop in lordly rule over many churches, which Scripture nowhere warrants. Christ feeds His sheep through a plurality of faithful undershepherds, who give account to the chief Shepherd alone.
roots_summary: From Latin sessio, “a sitting”; the sitting of the elders to govern the congregation.
roots_lines: Session — from Latin sessio, “a sitting.”
It is the local court of the elders in Presbyterian polity.
It is made up of the minister and ruling elders.
It rests on the New Testament plurality of elders.
The Baptist holds the elders govern within the congregation itself.
usage: Like the session, Christ rules His church by a plurality of godly elders, not one lord nor the crowd.
The session teaches the duty of elders to feed the flock and take the oversight willingly (1Pe 5:2).
The Baptist honours the Presbyterian eldership while confessing the congregation's own authority under Christ.

etymology: From Martin Luther, the German reformer whose recovery of the gospel shaped the worship of the churches that bear his name.
biblical_def: Lutheran worship is the worship of the churches gathered upon the teaching of Martin Luther, the reformer through whom God in 1517 began to call His church back to the gospel of justification by faith alone. The dictionary honours much in Luther’s recovery: he tore down the false sacrifice of the Mass, restored the cup to the people, set the preaching of the word at the centre, gave the Scriptures to the common man in his own tongue, and filled the church again with congregational hymn-singing, that the whole people might praise God with understanding. For these mercies the church is forever in his debt. Yet Lutheran worship retained corruptions the further Reformation cast off. In the Supper it confessed consubstantiation, a sacramental union in which the body and blood of Christ are held to be present in, with, and under the bread and wine, against the Reformed reading of Christ’s words, “this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24–26). And in worship it kept the “normative principle,” permitting whatever Scripture does not forbid — retaining altars, images, candles, and ceremonies — against the regulative principle, that God may be worshipped only as He has commanded. The Lord saith, “What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto” (Deu 12:32), and forbids the graven image and the worshipping of God by men’s devices (Exo 20:4–5). True worshippers worship the Father in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24).
webster_summary: The worship of the Lutheran churches, honoured for Luther's gospel recovery but corrupted by consubstantiation and the normative principle.
webster_full: LUTHERAN WORSHIP, the worship of the churches founded on Luther's teaching.
It rightly recovered justification by faith and the preaching of the word.
It restored congregational hymn-singing and the Scriptures in the common tongue.
Yet it confessed consubstantiation, a sacramental union in the Supper.
And it kept the normative principle, retaining altars, images, and ceremonies.
scriptures: Joh 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
corruption_summary: Honoured for Luther's gospel recovery, Lutheran worship is corrupted by consubstantiation in the Supper and the normative principle against the regulative.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption in Lutheran worship is twofold, and the dictionary names it as error, not difference. First, in the Lord’s Supper, Lutheranism confessed consubstantiation, the sacramental union, holding that the very body and blood of Christ are present in, with, and under the bread and wine, received by the mouth of all communicants. This corrupts the Supper, which is a memorial sign-and-seal wherein Christ is spiritually present to the believer by faith; the Lord said “this do in remembrance of me,” and His glorified body is in heaven, not enclosed in the elements upon ten thousand altars.

Second, Lutheran worship kept the normative principle, the rule that whatever Scripture does not expressly forbid may be retained in worship; and so it kept altars, crucifixes, images, vestments, and ceremonies inherited from Rome. Against this stands the regulative principle, the great recovery of the Reformed and Puritan church: that God may be worshipped only in the ways He has appointed, for what He has not commanded in His worship He has forbidden. “Thou shalt not add thereto” (Deu 12:32). Luther swept much filth from the church; it remained for the further Reformation to sweep the rest, and to worship the Father in spirit and in truth, after His command alone.
roots_summary: Named from Martin Luther, whose gospel recovery shaped the worship of the churches that bear his name.
roots_lines: Lutheran — from Martin Luther, the German reformer.
Luther recovered justification by faith alone in 1517.
He restored congregational hymn-singing and the word preached.
Lutheran worship confessed consubstantiation in the Supper.
It kept the normative principle, retaining images and ceremonies.
usage: Honour Luther's recovery of the gospel, yet test his worship by the command of God, not the leave of man.
Lutheran worship warns that a half-reformation in worship leaves the leaven of Rome behind.
The regulative principle teaches that what God has not commanded in His worship, He has forbidden.

etymology: From Latin Anglicanus, “English,” the worship of the Church of England framed in the English Reformation.
biblical_def: Anglican worship is the worship of the Church of England as it took form in the English Reformation under Thomas Cranmer, archbishop and martyr, who framed the Book of Common Prayer and set the English liturgy in the people’s own tongue. The dictionary honours much here: Cranmer’s labour to give England the Scriptures and prayers in English, the deep and reverent cadences of the Prayer Book steeped in the very words of Scripture, the Thirty-Nine Articles that confess a largely Reformed doctrine of grace, and above all the English martyrs — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and the hundreds burned under Mary — who loved not their lives unto the death. Latimer’s word at the stake, that they should this day light such a candle as should never be put out, is a treasure of the church. Yet Anglican worship retained corruptions the fuller Reformation rejected. It kept prelacy, the rule of bishops in a hierarchy above the presbyters, a government Scripture nowhere commands. It prescribed set ceremonies, vestments, kneeling, and a fixed liturgy beyond what the word warrants. And it embraced the way of compromise, the via media or middle road, seeking to stand between Rome and the Reformation rather than to be reformed wholly by the word. Against all this stands the regulative principle, that God must be worshipped as He has commanded (Deu 12:32), in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:23–24), lest men teach for doctrines the commandments of men (Mat 15:9).
webster_summary: The worship of the Church of England, honoured for Cranmer, the Prayer Book, and the martyrs, but corrupted by prelacy, ceremonialism, and the via media.
webster_full: ANGLICAN WORSHIP, the worship of the Church of England.
It was framed by Cranmer in the English Reformation and the Book of Common Prayer.
Its Prayer Book cadences and Thirty-Nine Articles are largely Reformed.
Yet it kept prelacy, the hierarchy of bishops above the presbyters.
And it kept prescribed ceremonies and the compromising via media.
scriptures: Joh 4:23
But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it.
Mat 15:9
But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.
corruption_summary: Honoured for Cranmer and the martyrs, Anglican worship is corrupted by prelacy, prescribed ceremonialism, and the via-media compromise.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption in Anglican worship the dictionary names plainly, while honouring the English Reformation’s true gains. First, it kept prelacy, the government of diocesan bishops set in lordly rule above the presbyters, an office Scripture nowhere commands; the New Testament uses bishop and elder for one office, and knows a plurality of elders, not a hierarchy of prelates. Second, it prescribed ceremonies, vestments, and a fixed liturgy beyond the warrant of the word, retaining forms the Puritans rightly judged to be the rags of Rome — teaching for doctrines the commandments of men (Mat 15:9).

Third, and most deeply, Anglican worship embraced the via media, the middle way, seeking to stand between Rome and the Reformation as a settlement of state rather than to be reformed wholly by Scripture. This compromise is named a corruption, not a virtue; it was this very middle road the Puritans laboured to reform further, and for which Nonconformists were ejected and persecuted. The principle to recover is the regulative principle: that the church is to worship the Father in spirit and in truth, by His command alone, and not after the tradition of men (Col 2:8). The English martyrs lit a candle that should never be put out; the fuller Reformation carried that flame against every relic of human invention in the worship of God.
roots_summary: From Latin Anglicanus, “English”; the worship of the Church of England framed in its Reformation.
roots_lines: Anglican — from Latin Anglicanus, “English.”
Cranmer framed the Book of Common Prayer and English liturgy.
The Thirty-Nine Articles confess a largely Reformed doctrine.
Anglican worship kept prelacy and prescribed ceremonies.
It embraced the via media, the compromising middle road.
usage: Honour Cranmer and the English martyrs, yet test Anglican worship by Scripture's command alone.
Anglican worship warns that a state-settled middle road leaves human invention in the house of God.
The regulative principle calls the church to worship the Father in spirit and in truth, not by men's traditions.

etymology: The sacred reckoning of Israel’s year, its feasts, new moons, and sabbaths appointed in the law of Moses.
biblical_def: The Jewish calendar is the sacred reckoning of Israel’s year, the appointed feasts, new moons, and sabbaths set forth in the law of Moses, chiefly in the twenty-third chapter of Leviticus. The year began in Abib, the month of the Passover, by the LORD’s command, “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months” (Exo 12:2). Through the year ran the great feasts of the LORD, holy convocations which Israel was to proclaim in their seasons (Lev 23:2): the Passover and Unleavened Bread, the Firstfruits and Pentecost, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles; with the weekly sabbath, the monthly new moons, and the sabbatical and jubilee years. These were not bare almanac days but a calendar of grace, each feast a shadow of good things to come, teaching Israel to number her days by the redeeming acts of God. The dictionary receives this calendar with reverence as God-given, and recovers its true meaning in Christ. For all these holy days were shadows, “but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:16–17): the Passover lamb is Christ our passover sacrificed for us; the firstfruits, His resurrection; Pentecost, the pouring out of His Spirit; the day of atonement, His once-for-all blood; the tabernacles, His dwelling with His people. Therefore the church is warned not to turn back to the weak and beggarly elements, observing days, and months, and times, and years as though the substance had not come (Gal 4:9–10).
webster_summary: The sacred year of Israel's feasts, new moons, and sabbaths (Lev 23), all shadows fulfilled in Christ, who is their substance (Col 2:17).

It set forth the appointed feasts, new moons, and sabbaths of the law (Lev 23).
The year began in Abib, the month of the Passover (Exo 12:2).
Its feasts were shadows of good things to come.
The body that casts them is Christ, their fulfilment (Col 2:17).

corruption_summary: A God-given calendar of shadows, not a contested doctrine; its feasts witness to Christ their substance, and warn against returning to the shadow.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the typology: the feasts, new moons, and sabbaths of Israel were shadows of good things to come, and the body that casts every shadow is Christ. The Passover was His sacrifice, the firstfruits His rising, Pentecost His outpoured Spirit, the day of atonement His blood, the tabernacles His dwelling with men. To read the calendar of Leviticus is to read a calendar of grace, every appointed season pointing forward to the Redeemer in whom all were fulfilled.

The caution the Scripture itself raises is the danger of turning back to the shadow now that the substance has come. The apostle warns the churches not to be brought again into bondage to the weak and beggarly elements, observing days, and months, and times, and years (Gal 4:9–10), nor to let any man judge them in respect of an holyday or the new moon or the sabbath days (Col 2:16). The dictionary honours the sacred year as God’s own gift to Israel, while confessing that its glory has passed into the greater glory of Christ, who is the true Passover, the true atonement, and the true rest of His people.
roots_summary: The appointed feasts, new moons, and sabbaths of Leviticus 23, the sacred year of Israel.
roots_lines: The Jewish Calendar — the sacred year of Israel's feasts.
Its appointed days are set forth chiefly in Leviticus 23.
The year began in Abib, the month of the Passover.
The feasts were holy convocations and shadows of things to come.
Their substance is Christ, who fulfilled them all.
usage: Like Israel's feasts, every shadow of the law points forward to Christ, who is their body and substance.
The calendar teaches the church not to turn back to the shadow now that the substance has come.
To read the sacred year aright is to read the gospel preached beforehand in feast and sabbath.

etymology: The fixed seasons of prayer marked in Scripture, the appointed times at which the godly turned to seek the LORD.
biblical_def: The hours of prayer are the fixed seasons at which the godly in Scripture turned to seek the LORD, the appointed times of daily devotion observed in Israel and in the apostolic church. David sang, “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice” (Psa 55:17), marking three set times of prayer in the day. Daniel, when the wicked decree was signed, opened his windows toward Jerusalem and kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime (Dan 6:10), holding fast his settled hours though it cost him the lions’ den. In the days of the apostles Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour (Act 3:1), and Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour (Act 10:9), when God gave him the vision that opened the gospel to the Gentiles. From such examples the church learned the wisdom of disciplined and ordered prayer, of fixed times set apart that the soul be not left to the chances of the day. The dictionary commends this discipline, for the praying soul is strengthened by appointed seasons of communion with God. Yet it warns against the corruption that turns fixed prayer into mechanical formalism, the vain repetitions that our Lord forbade: “use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7). The hour is the servant of prayer, not its master; the heart, not the clock, makes the prayer.
webster_summary: The fixed seasons of prayer in Scripture — evening, morning, noon, the ninth hour — honoured as discipline yet guarded from mechanical formalism.
webster_full: THE HOURS OF PRAYER, the fixed seasons of daily devotion in Scripture.
David prayed evening, morning, and at noon (Psa 55:17).
Daniel kneeled and prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem (Dan 6:10).
Peter and John went to the temple at the ninth hour of prayer (Act 3:1).
Such discipline is commended, yet guarded from vain repetition (Mat 6:7).

corruption_summary: A discipline of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to ordered prayer, while warning against mechanical formalism and vain repetition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the wisdom of disciplined, ordered prayer. David, Daniel, and the apostles kept fixed seasons of devotion, set times each day to seek the LORD; and the soul is strengthened by such appointed hours, lest prayer be left to the shifting chances of a busy day. Daniel held his three times of prayer though it cost him the lions’ den; the godly do well to set their own appointed seasons of communion with God, that the habit of prayer be not lost in the press of the world.

The caution bound up with this discipline is the danger of formalism, when the fixed hour becomes a mechanical rite emptied of living faith. Our Lord forbade the vain repetitions of the heathen, who think to be heard for their much speaking (Mat 6:7). The hour is the servant of prayer, not its master; it is the heart poured out before God, not the striking of the clock, that makes the prayer. The dictionary commends ordered times of devotion while warning that no schedule of prayer can stand for the broken and contrite heart that God will not despise.

usage: Like David and Daniel, set apart fixed seasons to seek the LORD, that prayer be not lost in the day's press.

Yet the hour is the servant of prayer, not its master; the broken heart, not the clock, makes the prayer.

etymology: The recovery of the gospel in Italy in the sixteenth century, crushed by Rome and the Inquisition, its exiles scattered through Reformed Europe.
biblical_def: The Italian Reformation was the brief and bright dawning of the gospel in sixteenth-century Italy, in the very shadow of Rome, before it was crushed by the Inquisition. Its chief lights were Peter Martyr Vermigli, the learned reformer who fled to teach at Strasbourg, Oxford, and Zurich, and Bernardino Ochino, the famed Capuchin preacher who left his order for the gospel; about them gathered a circle at Naples under Juan de Valdés, where many noble souls came to taste justification by faith alone. Behind them stood the ancient endurance of the Waldensians, the “poor men of Lyons,” who in the valleys of Piedmont had held to a simpler faith for three centuries before Luther, and who in 1532 cast in their lot with the Reformation. But Rome would not suffer the light. The Roman Inquisition, set up afresh in 1542, hunted the evangelicals through the peninsula; the Index forbade their books; the Waldensian valleys were drenched in blood in massacre after massacre. The Italian Reformation was crushed at home, yet its exiles enriched the churches of Geneva, Zurich, and England, carrying their gifts where they could freely worship. They overcame by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony, and loved not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11); for all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution (2Ti 3:12); and of such, of whom the world was not worthy, they wandered in deserts, in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth (Heb 11:37–38).
webster_summary: The sixteenth-century recovery of the gospel in Italy — Vermigli, Ochino, the Waldensians — crushed by Rome, its exiles enriching Reformed Europe.
webster_full: THE ITALIAN REFORMATION, the gospel's dawning in sixteenth-century Italy.

Crushed by Rome and the Inquisition, its exiles enriched Reformed Europe.

corruption_summary: The gospel's brief dawn in Italy was crushed by Roman corruption and the Inquisition, yet its martyrs and exiles enriched the Reformed church.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption the Italian Reformation suffered under was the Roman Church itself, which would not endure the recovered gospel in its own homeland. When justification by faith began to be preached at Naples and Lucca and through the peninsula, Rome answered not with Scripture but with the sword. The Roman Inquisition was newly armed in 1542 to hunt down the evangelicals; the Index of forbidden books strangled their writings; and the ancient Waldensian valleys of Piedmont, which had kept a purer faith for centuries before Luther, were given over to massacre. This persecution the dictionary names as the corruption of a church that defended its errors with blood rather than confess them and be reformed.

Yet the LORD turned the cruelty of Rome to the enriching of His church. The exiles driven out of Italy — Vermigli, Ochino, and many another — carried their learning and their faith to Geneva, Zurich, Strasbourg, and England, strengthening the Reformation where it could stand. The blood of the Waldensian martyrs, of whom the world was not worthy, became seed; for they overcame by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, and loved not their lives unto the death. The dictionary honours these martyrs and exiles, and names the persecution that scattered them for what it was: the corruption of Rome resisting the gospel of grace.
roots_summary: The sixteenth-century recovery of the gospel in Italy, named for the land where it briefly shone.
roots_lines: The Italian Reformation — the gospel's dawning in Italy.
